lead: A charter yacht lives on her batteries from the moment the shore cable comes off. At check-in you find out how the banks are split, what each breaker feeds and what the numbers mean; during the week you spend amp-hours like fuel.

sections.title: Two banks, kept apart

qa.q: Why does a charter yacht have separate engine and house batteries?
qa.a: So a **house bank** flattened overnight still leaves the engine able to start: each engine has its own starter battery, and the house bank runs everything else. Switch to BOTH only to start on a flat battery.

refs: Battery switches — after a parallel start

blocks.p: Each engine has its own **starter battery**; the **house bank** runs everything else. Kept separate, a house bank flattened overnight still leaves the engine able to start. On a catamaran ask which alternator charges the house bank: often only one does.

fig.title: Battery switches
lines: ENGINE, HOUSE: on at sea and at anchor
BOTH: only to start on a flat battery
Then BOTH off and an hour's charge

blocks.p: Switching the engine battery off while the engine runs can wreck the alternator. Terminals should be clean, tight and covered: a spanner dropped across them starts a fire, so tightening them is the base's job. Learn where the master switches are, for the dark.
Leave the battery vent open: batteries on charge give off hydrogen. A hot, bulging battery that smells of rotten eggs is being overcharged: charger off, hatches open, no sparks, call the base.

qa.q: At what voltage do the boat's batteries need charging?
qa.a: At about **12.2 V** on a rested lead-acid bank: that is half charge, time to charge. 12.7 V is full and 12.0 V or less is flat; read it only after an hour with no charge and no load.

blocks.p: The voltmeter tells the state of a lead-acid bank only when the bank has **rested**: no charge and no load for an hour or so.

On shore power or with the engine running you read the charger, not the battery: up to 14.4 V in bulk, 13.8 V on FLOAT, when the bank is full. Lower volts with the amps negative mean nothing is charging.

lines: Belt or alternator: before you leave

blocks.p: A **battery monitor** counts amp-hours out and in since the last full charge: 76 Ah used from a 200 Ah bank is 62 %. If it says 100 % while the volts say 12.1, it has lost count: believe the volts. A lithium bank is the opposite: it holds about 13 V until nearly empty, so trust the percentage.
An old bank that falls to 11.9 V after a quiet night has lost its capacity. If the alternator fails mid-week: cut every load, make for shore power, call the base.

qa.q: How many amp-hours can I actually use from a 200 Ah battery bank?
qa.a: About 100 Ah: only half of a lead-acid bank is usable between charges. Budget in **amp-hours**, current times time: a fridge drawing 5 A for 10 hours takes 50 Ah.

blocks.p: Current times time gives **amp-hours**. Only half of a lead-acid bank is usable, so a 200 Ah bank gives you about 100 Ah between charges.

fig.title: One night at anchor
lines: Anchor light and phones: a few Ah more
Morning: run the engine for an hour

blocks.p: With no solar and no generator, plan an hour of engine morning and evening and switch off what is not in use. A solar controller showing +7 A at 13.9 V is charging, but three fridges drawing 12 A round the clock take about 290 Ah a day, more than the sun gives back. Before a windy passage charge full: autopilot, plotter, VHF and bilge pump all run on that bank.

The 230 V sockets are live only on shore power or a generator. An **inverter** makes 230 V from the batteries, at a price: a 1,600 W hairdryer draws about 140 A (1,600 ÷ 12 = 133 A, plus the inverter's losses). A small one runs a laptop, not a kettle, and left on idle it still takes about 1 A: 24 Ah a day.

qa.q: How do I connect shore power safely in a marina?
qa.a: With the boat's 230 V main off, plug in at the boat end, then the pedestal, then switch the pedestal on; the 230 V main and the charger go on last. Never hold a **live plug**.

blocks.p: 230 V on a wet pontoon can kill. Never hold a live plug, never accept a cable with a cut sheath, and never push bare wires into a pedestal: ask the marina office for an adapter.

blocks.p: Watts divided by 230 give amps: a 1,200 W water heater, a 2,000 W kettle and a 500 W charger together draw 16 A, too much for a 10 A pedestal. Keep the cable out of the water; nobody swims in a marina: stray current kills.

sections.title: Every breaker shown, every light seen

qa.q: Which breakers should stay on overnight at anchor?
qa.a: Three: the **anchor light**, the bilge pump and the gas alarm. The all-round white anchor light burns every night at anchor (COLREGs Rule 30).

blocks.p: Have each breaker switched on in turn: you will be looking for them at night. Test the lights after dark, from the pontoon.

At anchor the **all-round white light** burns every night (COLREGs Rule 30). If it fails, hang a white lamp in the foretriangle; nobody climbs the mast in the dark. Overnight three breakers stay on: anchor light, bilge pump, gas alarm.

list: Bilge pump: switch to ON and hear it, lift the float to prove AUTO, find the hand-pump handle. Running in a dry bilge, its float is stuck: pump off, check the bilge by eye, call the base.
Gas and CO alarms: press TEST on each.
Windlass: engine running whenever you use it.
Electric winch: everyone knows where its isolator is.
Generator: its exhaust carries carbon monoxide; nobody swims at the stern while it runs.

qa.q: What do I do if a fuse keeps blowing on a charter boat?
qa.a: Fit a spare of the same rating, never a bigger one; if it blows again, leave it out and call the base. A **fuse** is there to stop the wire overheating.

blocks.p: A breaker resets; a fuse needs a spare, so ask where the spares are kept. Both are there to stop a wire overheating.

blocks.p: Instruments dead by day? Steer by compass and paper chart, and ring the base.
